reconcile.connective: The commentators read the "angel of the LORD" and the "God" who speaks as one and the same, the angel being the visible form in which God himself is present.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses the plain shift of speakers, listing Exodus 3:2 and Acts 7:35 (an angel) against Exodus 3:4 and Mark 12:26 (God) as two different answers to one question.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Who appeared to Moses in the burning bush?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/bush.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; contra/bush.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The transition from the Angel of Jehovah (Exo 3:2) to Jehovah (Exo 3:4) proves the identity of the two; and the interchange of Jehovah and Elohim, in Exo 3:4, precludes the idea of Jehovah being merely a national God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the angel-vs-God tension: the very shift from 'Angel of Jehovah' (3:2) to 'Jehovah/God' (3:4) is read as proof of identity, not a change of speaker. Strongest single reconcile.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Here the preternatural fire may be primarily meant by the expression "angel of the Lord"; but it is clear that under this symbol, the Divine Being was present, whose name is given (Exo 3:4, Exo 3:6), and elsewhere called the angel of the covenant, Jehovah-Jesus.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly says the 'angel of the Lord' of 3:2 is the symbol under which the Divine Being himself was present, naming 3:4 as where that name is given — collapsing the two speakers into one.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Whom he calleth the Angel, verse 2.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Annotates the 'God called' verse (3:4) by pointing back to 'the Angel' of 3:2 — a compact, distinct-voice cross-identification of the God who speaks with the angel who appeared.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on Exodus 3:2
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Treats this exact tension at the verse, reading the Angel-of-Jehovah/Jehovah-Elohim alternation as proof of a single divine speaker rather than two. (Haley's coverage of this specific passage could not be confirmed; per spec a row-surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage is used.)
